title: After AI Takes the Talent, Only Six Tokens Are Left to Own
dek: Delphi's Yan Liberman says crypto VCs make one deal a year because AI has sucked up all the smart people; the only real money left is in a handful of tokens with real revenue that don't depend on crypto markets.
why: A frontline crypto VC publicly lays out his six positions and his reasoning, including why he no longer does crypto venture and why he has given up on gaming. High information density, but you need some crypto background.
who: Crypto fund managers, token investors, and anyone who wants to understand how a frontline crypto VC allocates capital and evaluates founders.
skip: The ad segment from 16:17 to 17:57 can be skipped.

points.h: This rally has no obvious buyer
points.body: Yan says the market was caught off guard by ‘QE in the form of long-end bond curve control’, which triggered a short squeeze, but he personally finds it hard to see new highs in the short term because it would take a lot of new money, and the obvious historical buyer (Sailor) isn't buying now — he's cashmaxing and paying down preferred stock. He thinks leverage hasn't built up excessively, and this sequence of slow grind, pause, alt rotation is actually healthy. Another structural change is that the alt market has gotten shallower, money concentrates more easily into a few assets, so you don't need a whole new cohort of buyers to move the market — it has become a ‘stock picker's market’.

points.h: Buy the ones that look like hot coins but aren't as crowded
points.body: Yan admits there are only about 10 to 15 investable liquid tokens right now, and every crypto fund is already positioned in those 15. His conclusion: you should look for names that ‘look and smell like these coins but aren't as crowded to trade’. Hyperliquid is a long-term bull, but going to 200 within four months would be a surprise; for short-term outperformance you have to look at less obvious names. Santi adds that with 15 investable coins, any liquid fund going on a show repeats the same five names.

points.h: Crypto venture does one deal a year
points.body: Yan says only one of their latest venture fund's five investments is crypto, and over the past year they did just one crypto venture deal. The reason is that value capture and defensibility in crypto venture are now clearer, so you can quickly filter out a large number of projects, but the thesis that ‘crypto gets broadly adopted across multiple verticals’ has been pushed to the sidelines, and AI is a major factor in drawing away talent, attention and capital. His one crypto investment is Tori Finance, a tokenized Turkish lira carry trade, dollar-hedged, about 10.5% organic yield, no incentives.

points.h: The six tokens share one thing: revenue not from crypto
points.body: Yan's six public tokens are Hyperliquid, Zcash, Lighter, Venice, Grass and Aerodrome. He says he prefers projects with a ‘revenue story’ that don't depend heavily on crypto activity, because that makes them more resilient and gives a stronger TAM story. He goes deep on Grass: projected $70 million revenue, $40 million operating profit, doing residential IP network data scraping for frontier labs as customers, token market cap $330 million, unlocks finished in October, about 30% of supply with the foundation, no equity only a foundation, and if valued as a pure equity non-crypto business it could probably raise $1 to 2 billion in the private market.

points.h: The return bar for crypto has changed
points.body: Yan says he no longer anchors on annualized return rates but instead sets individual price targets, stop losses and invalidation conditions, and keeps a reserve of cash for a ‘total collapse’ scenario. He admits he just likes volatility. Santi says he now won't do crypto venture that can't at least 10x, that Ethereum at a $300 billion market cap shows no clean 10x, and that the downside asymmetry is far greater than the upside. Yan responds that comfort comes from holding ‘productive assets’ rather than ‘reflexive assets’, and the key to a productive asset is the durability of its earnings and how much it depends on reflexive assets.

points.h: The gaming vertical has been given up
points.body: Yan says gaming as a whole is a hard vertical to invest in because games as businesses have too short a lifecycle, and once you run the NPV the long-term value story is hard to sustain. They tried Gunzilla, a big bet, and it didn't go well — he attributes that to management and spending issues, not game quality; the game itself is AAA level, on par with Call of Duty, PUBG and Fortnite. He says this may be their last attempt at AAA level, and after that gaming as a broad category will be hard, with only small-format games doing well. They now think the only truly investable vertical left is basically ‘financialized applications’.

points.h: Aerodrome is a classic catch-up trade
points.body: Yan says Aerodrome had planned to migrate to mainnet in mid-July and support multichain, but it was delayed and the price suffered as a result; the launch is now set for the second half of September, migration to ETH and ARC has been announced, and whether it migrates to Robin Hood is unconfirmed. He sees this as a huge opportunity for TVL, volume and fees, and many people treat it as a catch-up trade. The prior problem was the relationship between emissions and revenue — emissions go to LPs, revenue goes to stakers, and it was criticized as offsetting revenue with emissions. Now they want to make emissions dynamic, tied one-to-one to trading volume, so price up means emissions down; at the same time they are adding multiple revenue lines, estimated to contribute an extra 40% of revenue with no emissions offset. Currently OI relative to market cap is not a large position.

points.h: The investment committee now weighs founders most
points.body: Yan says if he could pick only one change, it's the weight given to founder due diligence. In crypto's early days it was obvious what needed to exist, so investing was more about the idea and defensibility, with lower founder weight. But once you move into other professional verticals, you can't really diligence the idea and moat, and the only repeatable, scalable thing is the founder side. They now ask ‘what is your earliest memory, then walk us through your life’. He also mentions the ‘chip on the shoulder’ from childhood trauma and the desperate desire to win as factors that are genuinely valuable, and gives Athena's Guy as an example, saying he will do whatever it takes to win.
